children.translated_text: Proof of the Non-authoritativeness of the Veda (<s>Vedāprāmāṇyasiddhi</s>)
That which has no connection
with something anywhere,
has no authoritativeness (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) there,
like a donkey that has no connection with fire.
And unconnected are
the Vedic
words with external objects — this is a negative concomitance through non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>).

children.text: na tāvad ayam asiddho hetuḥ | śabdānām artheṣu

children.translated_text: no connection
with objects. For connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) means being of a connected nature (<s>pratibaddhasvabhāvatā</s>).
And

children.text: ca sā nirnibandhanā sarveṣāṃ sarvatra pratibaddhasvabhāvatā
children.translated_text: that [connected nature] is not without a basis (<s>nirnibandhanā</s>), because there would be the absurd consequence of everything being connected with everything.
And the basis of this cannot be established as anything other than identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) and causal origination (<s>tadutpatti</s>),
because that which is not of that nature and not originated from that
is of unconnected nature with respect to it. And
words do not have the nature of external objects,
because they are objects of cognition that manifests differently [from the objects]. Nor do words arise from external objects,
because the production of words is observed even without an object, since a person's speech-activity is connected with
his will.
Because the production of words [independent of objects] is observed.
This reason (<s>hetu</s>) is not unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>), because words have in reality
just as the eye-faculty
with respect to form.
The eye,
when functioning, causes the apprehension of form alone. Similarly, these
Vedic
words, even though devoid of identity and causal origination [with their objects], will reveal supersensory
objects through mere capacity alone.
How then, merely by the absence of identity and causal origination,
is there non-connection,
so that this
negative concomitance through non-apprehension of the pervader would be established?
[Objection:] But something is observed to be of connected nature with something somewhere through mere capacity (<s>yogyatā</s>) alone,
not a fault. Because the eye-faculty too, setting aside taste and the rest,
is restricted to being an illuminator of form alone, since it is an effect of that [form].
For form
assists the eye. The eye does not
illuminate form by mere existence alone,

because there would be the absurd consequence of apprehending even an occluded form. Therefore, having attained the capacity to generate knowledge of form from a form that is present at an appropriate location,
the eye
produces a visual cognition

children.text: utpādayat tatkāryam iti vyaktam avasīyate | anyathā
children.translated_text: — and it is clearly ascertained that it is an effect of that [form]. Otherwise,
for one not dependent on that [form's] assistance, its restriction to illuminating that alone cannot be established.
For in the absence of any distinction regarding being-not-assisted,
the restriction that the eye is an illuminator only of form
and not of taste and so forth
cannot be maintained. Well then, whence comes
this restriction
that
the eye is to be assisted by form alone and not
by taste and the rest?
This is

children.text: yadi vastuvaśād eva rūpam upakaroti na rasādikaṃ hanta

children.translated_text: just as there is a restriction regarding what can be assisted,
which is natural
for the eye

children.text: rūpeṇa tathā śabdānām api svābhāvika evāstu bahirarthapra
children.translated_text: with respect to form, similarly for words too let there be a natural restriction in revealing external objects.
If by the force of reality itself form assists [the eye] and taste etc. do not, well then,
Because nothing can be established as having a natural property. For
those who accept naturalness as a property of a thing
are to be
questioned:

children.text: | kiṃ svābhāvika iti svato bhavati | āhosvit parato
children.translated_text: Does 'natural' mean it arises from itself, or does it arise
from something else,
or is it simply without a cause?
If, first,

children.text: svato bhavati tad asaṅgataṃ svātmani kriyāviro
children.translated_text: it arises from itself — that is incoherent, because of the contradiction of action upon
oneself. Or if it is without a cause —
that is
improper, because without a cause the restriction to a particular place and time
cannot be established. Therefore the restriction of the eye to being assisted by form is not natural.
On what basis then?
We say: it is connected with its own cause (<s>svahetu</s>).

children.text: brūmaḥ | cakṣuḥ khalu svahetunā janyamānaṃ tādṛśam eva janitaṃ
children.translated_text: The eye, being produced by its own cause, is produced as precisely such that it can only be assisted by form. Form too is produced by its own cause as precisely such

children.text: yad rūpopakartavyam eva bhavati | rūpam api tādṛśam eva sva
children.translated_text: that it is of a nature that assists
that [eye].
[Reply:] Here it is said: The restriction of the eye being assisted by form is not natural.

children.text: śabdānām api sa svabhāvaḥ svahetupratibaddha eva

children.translated_text: by which they
are unfailing with respect to external objects.
[Objection:] Words too have that nature, connected with their own cause,
be maintained, because of the accepted eternality of Vedic sentences.
If, however, non-eternality
is accepted [for Vedic words], and one wishes to resolve this objection —

children.text: tad api duṣkaraṃ doṣāntaraprasaṅgāt | yadi svahetunaiva te
children.translated_text: that too is difficult, because of the consequence of another fault. If they were produced by their own cause with the power of revealing a determinate object,
then even one who has not learned the convention

children.text: syāpi svārtham avabodhayeyuḥ | yathā cakṣuḥ svaheto
children.translated_text: would understand their meaning, just as the eye, produced from its own cause as an illuminator of form,

children.text: prakāśakam utpannaṃ sat prakāśayaty eva rūpam asaṅketa
children.translated_text: being produced, illuminates form even for one

children.text: vido 'pi | na ca śabdād uccaritād api
children.translated_text: who does not know any convention. But there is no
understanding of a specific meaning for one who has not previously learned the convention,
even when a word is uttered. Therefore the conclusion is that there is no restriction in words conveying meaning that is connected with their own cause, as in the case of the eye
and so forth.
[Reply:] This cannot

children.text: atha svahetubhir evāyam īdṛśas teṣāṃ datto

children.translated_text: assignment

children.text: yena te saṅketaviśeṣasahāyā eva kam apy artham avabodhayanti |
children.translated_text: has been given to them, by which they reveal some object only with the assistance of a particular convention.
[Objection:] But it is precisely by their own causes that this kind of
they should function for different objects.

children.text: yuḥ | yadi hy ayam agnihotraśabdaḥ saṅketāpekṣo yāgaviśeṣapra
children.translated_text: For if this word '<s>agnihotra</s>' reveals a particular sacrifice depending on a convention,
how can it reveal a different object when the convention is different?

children.text: na hi kṣityādyapekṣeṇa bījena svahetor aṅkurajanakasvabhāve
children.translated_text: For a seed, produced from its own cause with the nature of generating a sprout in dependence on earth and the like,
cannot produce a donkey.
Similarly, a word too
should illuminate only that object to which it is restricted in conveying.
[Reply:] Then, when the convention is changed,
various conventions.
[Objection:] But it is said that this [word] is produced as merely capable of conveying various meanings depending on

children.text: tad api na prastutopayogi | na hy evam asya prāmāṇyam

children.translated_text: For when the conveyance of meaning intended by another person through convention
is indeed conceivable,
then it is
impossible to determine

children.text: kim ayam abhimatasyaivārthasya dyotako na veti |
children.translated_text: whether this [word] reveals only the intended meaning or not.
[Reply:] That too is not useful for the matter at hand. For in this way its authoritativeness (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) does not stand.
[Objection:] Then the relation of words and objects will be of the nature of signifier and signified (<s>vācyavācaka</s>). And thus it is said:
'Even if the relations of signifier and signified are real,
without being manifested through conventions, they are not causes of the manifestation of meaning.'
[Reply:]
the meaning —
this has been stated.
And when convention is required, [the words] should not function
for a different
object —
this and so forth
has been stated.
Therefore this signifier-signified relation has already been refuted.

children.text: vācyavācakalakṣaṇaḥ saṃbandhaḥ | tasmān na bahirarthe prati

children.translated_text: Therefore the conclusion is that words have no connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) with external objects.
But if that [relation] were real, even one who does not know the convention would understand
And therefore the reason (<s>hetu</s>) is not unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>).
And the absence of that [concomitance with the opposite] is demonstrated by showing its presence in the <s>sapakṣa</s> (similar instances).
For it is not proper for a contradictory [reason] to be present in a subject that possesses the property to be proved.
Because the opposite of what is to be proved is absent there.
And without the pervader, the pervaded cannot exist,
because there would be the consequence of it losing its status.
Nor is this reason inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>),
because of the existence of a defeater (<s>bādhaka</s>) in the case of the opposite.
When the negation of authoritativeness is what is to be proved,
authoritativeness itself is the dissimilar instance (<s>vipakṣa</s>).

children.text: na ca tasmin pratibandhābhāvalakṣaṇo hetur asti | svaviruddhena
children.translated_text: And the reason, characterized by the absence of connection, is not present there, because it is pervaded by connection, which is contrary to it. This word '<s>pramāṇa</s>' (valid cognition) is certainly not arbitrary among cognitions, without any basis.

children.text: pratibandhena vyāptatvāt | na khalv ayaṃ prādeśikaḥ pramāṇa
śabdaḥ jñāneṣu nirnibandhana eva | sarvajñāneṣu pramāṇavya
children.translated_text: For there would be the absurd consequence of designating all cognitions as <s>pramāṇa</s>.
And the basis cannot be established as anything other than connection with its own object.
Therefore, the fact that a <s>pramāṇa</s> is designated as '<s>pramāṇa</s>' is pervaded by
the existence of connection with its own object.
Therefore, through the apprehension of the pervaded of the contradictory (<s>viruddhavyāptopalambha</s>),

children.text: pramāṇe dharmiṇi vipakṣe prāmāṇyasya viruddhavyāptasyopalambhena vipakṣe vyava°

children.translated_text: since the exclusion from the <s>vipakṣa</s> (dissimilar instance) is established, the reason is not inconclusive.

children.text: na cānyo doṣaḥ saṃbhavī | tasmān nirastāśeṣadoṣeṇa hetunā yat
children.translated_text: Nor is any other fault possible. Therefore, what is established by a reason free from all faults is to be accepted by the wise.

children.text: prasiddhaṃ tad upādeyam eva satām iti |

children.translated_text: Nor is it contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>), because of the absence of concomitance with the opposite.
The <s>Vedāprāmāṇyasiddhi</s> (Proof of the Non-authoritativeness of the Veda), a composition of the learned <s>Jitāri</s>, is complete.
